content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide. The bird is raised in many climates, and its meat is prized for its mild flavor, moderate fat content, and high protein level. Chicken can be used in a huge variety of dishes, from soups and salads to casseroles and grilled preparations.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken provides all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.
The skin is edible and, when cooked properly, becomes crispy and rich in collagen.
Breast meat is the most popular cut, but thighs, drumsticks and wings are also heavily used.
Chicken is a staple in many diet plans because of its low fat content, especially skin‑less breast.
Different cultures have signature cooking methods, ranging from deep‑frying to slow braising in sauces.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken delivers a large amount of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat (skin‑less breast)
items.content: Skin‑less breast meat contains very little saturated fat, making it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The meat provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The high protein content helps keep you feeling full longer, which can aid weight management.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter, so it should be cooked to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Bird protein allergy
items.content: A small number of people can develop allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in processed products
items.content: Chicken sausages, deli meats and ready‑to‑eat dishes often contain high levels of salt, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Fat in the skin
items.content: Chicken skin is high in saturated fat; excessive consumption may raise cholesterol levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken can be grilled, baked, boiled, fried or stewed. Breast meat is common in salads, sandwiches and low‑fat meals. Thighs and drumsticks are ideal for roasting with herbs and spices. The skin can be crisped and added to soups or salads for extra flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh chicken should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C and used within 2 days. Frozen chicken retains quality for up to 9 months at –18 °C. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or a grayish color; discard if any signs of spoilage are present.
